rv.q: Philip Breen's direction ticks like clockwork, slyly hints at their class duality.
But who cares when the writing is great, the team effort in making the play work is admirable, and you have standout performances from Allam and Gillen?

cn.t: Ayckbourn's ingenious 1969 farce delights with its technically daring dual-dinner-party structure and Roger Allam's masterful comic performance, though darker themes of misogyny and marital despair now resonate more uncomfortably beneath the laughs.
